hints: Look at what a capillary has to do. It is the site of exchange, so think about how thick its wall needs to be for diffusion to be fast.
Recall which tissues give arteries and veins strength and control (muscle for constriction, elastic for stretch, collagen for toughness) and ask if a tiny exchange vessel needs them.
walkthrough:
**Remember the job of a capillary**

Think exchange, not transport. Capillaries deliver glucose and oxygen to tissues and pick up carbon dioxide and other wastes.

For this to happen quickly by diffusion, the wall must be as thin as possible.

**Build the thinnest possible wall**

The wall is just one cell thick. It is made of a single layer of flat squamous cells called endothelium, plus a very thin basement membrane.

There is no room or need for extra thick layers.

**Rule out the large-vessel tissues**

Smooth muscle is for vasoconstriction, elastic tissue is for stretching under high pressure, and collagen fibres are for resisting tearing. Those are vital in arteries, arterioles and veins.

Capillaries are tiny, low pressure vessels for exchange, so they lack all three. That matches row A only.

options.A: Correct. Capillary walls contain only endothelium (one cell thick) for rapid diffusion, with no smooth muscle, elastic tissue or collagen fibres.
options.B: Not correct. Endothelium is present, but collagen fibres are not a structural layer of the capillary wall.
options.C: Not correct. Capillaries must have endothelium, and they do not have smooth muscle or collagen in their walls.
options.D: Not correct. Capillaries lack both smooth muscle and elastic tissue, and they must contain endothelium.
